title: Psalm 62: My Soul Finds Rest in God Alone
summary: David declares that his soul waits quietly for God alone, his rock, salvation, and fortress, while enemies try to topple him with lies. He calls the people to trust God and pour out their hearts to him, warns that human status and wealth are only a breath, and closes with a twofold word he has heard: power belongs to God, and so does loving devotion.
story: Psalm 62 sits within the group of Davidic trust psalms in 61 to 64, and it may be the calmest of them. Where earlier psalms in Book II cry out for help, this one speaks from a settled confidence that has already found its footing. It also turns outward: after speaking to his own soul, David addresses the people and then teaches them what trust rules out. In that sense the psalm is both a prayer and a lesson in wisdom, close in tone to Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. Its closing confession about power and love anticipates the praise of God's might and kindness that fills Psalms 65 to 68.
historical:
The heading names David and adds “According to Jeduthun.” Jeduthun was one of the Levitical music leaders David appointed, along with Asaph and Heman (1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 25:1-6), and his name also appears in the headings of Psalms 39 and 77. The phrase may mean the psalm belonged to the repertoire of Jeduthun's guild or was sung in a style associated with him. The psalm gives no specific occasion. Its picture of a man of high position whom others are trying to push down from his lofty perch, with smiling mouths and hidden curses, has led some interpreters to connect it with the conspiracy of Absalom (2 Samuel 15), when trusted advisers turned against David. That setting is a reasonable suggestion but not stated in the text.

The warning against trusting in extortion and stolen goods reflects the constant temptation of powerful people in Israel to use their position to enrich themselves, a sin that the prophets condemned repeatedly (Isaiah 5:8; Micah 2:1-2). The psalm's wisdom applies in any period.
cultural:
Verse 3 pictures a leaning wall or a tottering fence. Walls in ancient Israel were often made of mudbrick or rough stone without mortar, and a wall that began to lean would soon fall. The enemies push against someone they think is already unstable. Verse 9 uses the image of merchants' scales. Goods were weighed on balance scales against stone weights, and the psalm says that if you put all people, high and low together, on one side of the scale, they would rise into the air because they weigh nothing. The word for their weightlessness, hevel, means breath or vapor.

Verse 11 uses a numerical saying, a device of Israel's wisdom teachers: “God has spoken once; I have heard this twice.” Similar patterns appear in Proverbs 6:16 and 30:15-31 and in Amos 1 and 2. The effect is emphasis: the lesson has been confirmed, and it is worth repeating.
literary: The psalm has three stanzas, each ending with Selah or a closing statement. Verses 1 to 4 speak of trust and then turn to address the enemies directly. Verses 5 to 8 repeat the opening with small but telling changes: “my salvation comes from Him” becomes “my hope comes from Him,” and “I will never be shaken” becomes “I will not be shaken.” This stanza ends by inviting the people to trust. Verses 9 to 12 draw wisdom lessons about human frailty and wealth and end with the double word about God's power and loving devotion. A small Hebrew word, akh, runs through the psalm six times. It can mean only, alone, or surely, and it gives the psalm its insistence: God alone, God only.

outline.t: My soul rests in God alone
Enemies who push, lie, and curse in secret
The soul told again to rest in God
An invitation to the people: pour out your hearts
People are a breath, riches are no refuge
Power and loving devotion belong to God

doctrines.note: Trust in this psalm is exclusive: God alone. It rules out trust in human status, in wealth, and in wrong gained by force. Faith is not only believing that God helps but refusing every rival refuge.

Verses 11 and 12 join two truths about God: power and loving devotion. His strength without love would be terrifying, and his love without strength would be helpless. Together they are the grounds for rest.
The psalm ends with God repaying each person according to his deeds. God's justice is part of the reason the trusting soul can be quiet: wrongs done in secret will be answered.

words.note: Akh, only, alone, surely. It appears six times in this short psalm, opening lines in verses 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, and 9. It drives home the psalm's point: God alone is the soul's rest and rock.

Dumiyyah, silence or stillness. Verse 1 says literally that the soul is silent toward God. The BSB renders it “finds rest.” It describes a quiet, waiting posture, not anxious agitation, the stillness of someone who has stopped fighting for their own security.

Hevel, breath, vapor. It is the key word of Ecclesiastes, often translated vanity or meaningless. In verse 9 all human beings, lowborn and exalted, are but a vapor. The point is not that people are worthless but that they are too light to trust as one's final security.

Shaphakh, to pour out. Verse 8 invites the people to “pour out your hearts before Him,” the language of emptying a vessel completely. Hannah used the same verb when she said she had poured out her soul before the LORD (1 Samuel 1:15).

christ: Jesus invited the weary to come to him and find rest for their souls (Matthew 11:28-29), offering in his own person the rest this psalm finds in God alone. Paul quotes the psalm's final line, that God will repay each person according to his deeds, in Romans 2:6, where it grounds his argument that all people stand accountable before God. The same idea appears in Jesus' words about the Son of Man coming in glory and rewarding each person according to what he has done (Matthew 16:27). For Christians, the power and loving devotion that belong to God are displayed together most fully in the cross and resurrection, where God's love is shown in weakness and his power in raising Christ from the dead.
questions: What does it look like for your soul to find rest in God alone? What other sources of security compete for that place in your life?
Verse 8 invites us to pour out our hearts before God. What makes that hard for you, and what would help?
The psalm says power and loving devotion both belong to God. Which of these do you find harder to believe about God right now?
